findings: All five designated images are substantive, upright and legible; no page is excluded inside this batch.
The diagrams on pages 72–75 were verbalized with the actor directions, legal-versus-economic distinction, no-direct-claim or no-off-balance boundary, and accounting consequence preserved.
The numerical examples 5,000/5,200, 5,000/5,100 and 100 loss were checked against the images; amounts, units and debit/credit direction are preserved.
Page 75 preserves the distinction between the debt-equity-swap ordinary repayment entry and the debt-to-capital entry, plus the creditor-side stock-at-acquisition-date-fair-value rule.
Page 76 is a theory disclosure list, not a question/answer or false-proposition layout; the three disclosure categories and the no-market-price equity exception are preserved.

positive_examples: LP principle and concession methods retain the legal creditor status, risk/economic-benefit test and alternative journal entries.
Debt assumption retains both the legal first-obligor boundary and the narrow concession condition based on an irrevocable trust and very low recourse.
Debt-equity swap retains extinguishment, fair-value consideration, allowance offset and loss presentation.
Note disclosures retain materiality, consolidated/separate presentation, fair-value exceptions and level breakdown.
negative_or_boundary_examples: An LP investor cannot directly demand principal from the debtor because the original creditor remains the legal creditor.
Debt assumption is not a legal bond redemption under the principle method even though the issuer is economically released from payment operations.
The debt-equity-swap diagram distinguishes cash repayment from issuing capital; the creditor's financial-asset extinguishment follows the debtor's extinguishment.
Market-price-unavailable shares are an exception to fair-value disclosure, with the instrument overview and balance-sheet amount disclosed instead.
